_comment: QUESTION — words only, no pictures, read as PAGES: the questions of one page sit in a column he scrolls, and he answers each in place.

Use it before anything is drawn, and for any point that is decided in words. Four or more questions belong here rather than in a chat message: a wall of one-liners assumes he remembers every one of them.

Every question is written for someone with NO context, in three parts: what exists today, what goes wrong, and what would change. Err on more questions per page — a page is a set he can hold in his head at once.

Two fields change HOW he answers, on this or any other slide. "pick": "several" lets him choose more than one of the options (clicking a chosen one again unpicks it). "answer": "words" makes the answer a line he types, with "prompt" as its placeholder — for a name or a piece of copy, where a list of options invented in advance would never hear the answer he actually wants.

"stage" (ask / design / contract / review / accept) at the top of the deck makes the build check this deck carries the slide that stage exists for. It never says which OTHER slides are allowed: one deck can ask a question, show a picture and define done.
title: Saved searches — the questions before anything is drawn
_comment_title: title: what this deck is about, in his words. It also titles the first page when no page marker comes before the first question.
_comment_key: key: a short name for this deck. His answers are saved under it.
_comment_out: out: the page build writes, beside this spec.
_comment_themes: themes: a words deck opens in whichever palette his app is on; this list is what the palette buttons offer.
_comment_no_pictures: No "images" and no "runs": nothing here is photographed, so a deck of questions names neither.

steps._comment: A YES / NO / DON'T KNOW question: no options, so the page offers those three answers. 'Don't know' is a real answer — it says the question is not ready.
steps._comment_id: id: your name for this question. It labels his answer, so keep it short and never reuse it.
steps._comment_words: words: true — this step has no picture at all. Without it a step that merely forgot its picture would render silently blank.
steps._comment_surface: surface: the part of the app the question is about, named the way he would name it.
steps.path: The search box at the top of the session list
steps._comment_path: path: where in the app that is.
steps.headline: Should a search you run often be saveable?
steps._comment_headline: headline: the question itself, in one sentence. 25 words at most, no code words.
steps.today: Searching your past sessions means typing the words again every time, and the box forgets them as soon as you close it.
steps._comment_today: today: what exists right now — which part of the app, and what it does for him. Write it as though he has never seen it.
steps.problem: A search you run every Monday costs the same typing every Monday, and a long one is easy to mistype.
steps._comment_problem: problem: what goes wrong, as HE experiences it. Not the code's problem.
steps.proposal: A search could be kept by name and re-run in one press. Yes starts the design; No drops it and nothing changes.
steps._comment_proposal: proposal: what would change, as he would notice it. On a Yes/No question, say here what each answer leads to.

steps._comment: A PAGE MARKER, not a question: it starts a new page. Everything after it, up to the next marker, is read together. There is no marker before Q-1 above, so the first page is titled with the deck's own title.
steps._comment_page: page: the page's title. It must say something — a blank one is a page he cannot tell from the one before it.
steps.intro: The first page decided that searches can be saved. These three decide where you would find them again.
steps._comment_intro: intro (optional): one line under the title, saying what this set of questions is for.

steps._comment: A PICK-ONE question: the options ARE the answers, so the page offers them plus Other. One option is allowed when it is the answer you propose; three is usually the most he can hold at once.
steps.path: The search box at the top of the session list
steps.headline: Where should a saved search appear once you have saved it?
steps.today: The search box is empty every time you open it, and there is nowhere in the app that lists searches.
steps.problem: A saved search nobody can find is a saved search nobody uses, so where it lives decides whether the feature is worth building.
steps.proposal: Three places it could live. Pick the one you would actually look in.

options._comment: One answer. Its pros and cons are about HIS experience, never about the code.
options._comment_id: id: your name for this answer. It is what gets recorded.
options.label: Under the search box
options._comment_label: label: the answer's name, two or three words. Never write '(recommended)' into it — set the flag below instead, so the page can badge it.
pros: It is in front of you at the moment you would want it.
Nothing new to learn and nowhere new to go.
options._comment_pros: pros: short lines about what he gains. One point per line.
cons: Pushes the results down by a row.
Room for about three before the list gets long.
options._comment_cons: cons: the same, for what it costs him.
options.measured: 3 saved searches before it needs scrolling
options._comment_measured: measured (optional): a number. Needs a digit in it.
options._comment_recommended: recommended: true on AT MOST ONE answer. The page badges it; say WHY in that answer's pros.

options.label: In the session list
pros: Sits beside your sessions, where you already look for old work.
Room for as many as you like.
cons: Mixes searches in with sessions, which are different things.
One more thing making the list longer.

options.label: In settings
options.summary: A list you manage in one place and rarely visit.
options._comment_summary: summary (optional): a sentence instead of, or beside, the lists — for an answer that does not need both.
pros: Out of the way; nothing else on screen gets busier.
cons: Two clicks and a screen change away from where you would use it.

steps._comment: A STATEMENT, not a question: something you are asserting, that he confirms or rejects. No 'today' field, so the page treats it as a thing to approve — and 'yes'/'no' rename the buttons.
steps.path: The search box at the top of the session list
steps.headline: A saved search re-runs against everything, including sessions made since you saved it.
steps.changed: Stated, not asked: a saved search keeps the words, not the results, so it always answers with today's sessions.
steps._comment_changed: changed: the What changed card. On a statement, what you are asserting.
steps.notice: The same saved search finds more as you work, and never shows a result you have deleted.
steps._comment_notice: notice: the You'll notice card — what this means for him in practice.
steps._comment_yes: yes (optional): renames the Yes button. Under five words. Use it when 'Yes, build it' is the wrong thing to say.
steps._comment_no: no (optional): renames the No button. Under five words.
